title: iPhone Duo inner-screen repair costs $999, more than twice the Galaxy Z Fold 8's cost
content: Apple has revealed repair costs for its first foldable smartphone, the iPhone Duo, ahead of its US launch on October 23, 2026. The company will charge $999 for the inner display, and repairs for certain other types of damage could cost up to $1,499, according to MacRumors . The repair fees are considerable for a device that costs $1,999. Meanwhile, Samsung's estimate for repairing the Galaxy Z Fold 8 in the United States is $419 to replace the inner screen, according to the company’s US repair pricing page. This indicates that the inner display repair price of the iPhone Duo is $580 higher than Samsung, suggesting the cost Apple could face to repair the foldable. iPhone Duo repair costs without AppleCare+ Apple's repair estimates are that the iPhone Duo 's inner display is $999 to replace, and damage classified as “other damage” is $1,499. The price of replacing the outer display is $379, while the rear camera and battery replacement fees are $229 each. Apple will sell the repair of the back glass for $199 and the replacement of the removable nano-texture cover layer over the display screen for $49 if the glass is not damaged. Here is the full list of repair charges without AppleCare+: Cover layer: $49 Back glass: $199 Battery service: $229 Rear camera: $229 Outer display: $379 Work area: $333 Inner display: $999 Other damage: $1,499 Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 repairs cost less The Galaxy Z Fold 8 inner-screen replacement is priced at $419 in the US, while the inner-screen replacement on the iPhone Duo costs $999. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra's inner-screen repair costs $479. The Samsung screen module replacement includes additional connected components, and for the Fold 8, it's priced at $579; the Fold 8 Ultra is $ 639. Also Read | Nothing CEO Carl Pei calls Apple iPhone Duo a ‘waste of money’: Here’s why Samsung is also bringing a first-time repair of the Galaxy Z TriFold's inner screen to its refurbished lineup at a promotional price of $699.50. This is a limited first-repair special but is still $299.50 below the iPhone Duo's inner screen replacement. AppleCare+ reduces iPhone Duo repair charges AppleCare + offers a lower-cost option for accidental damage. Coverage for the iPhone Duo costs $19.99 per month, $199.99 annually or $399 upfront. With AppleCare+, inner-display repairs and other accidental-damage repairs cost $99 each. Outer-display and back-glass repairs cost $29, and cover-layer replacement costs $19. If the battery has less than 80% of the original capacity, the battery service is free. A $149 fee applies to theft or loss claims. Also Read | iPhone 17 Pro under ₹1 lakh? Check Croma, Amazon and Flipkart festive offers The iPhone Duo will go on pre-order on Friday, October 16, and will be released on October 23, 2026. The price of coverage will need to be balanced with the potential cost of repairing the foldable without coverage.

title: Global financial watchdog calls for more human oversight of agentic AI
content: LONDON, Oct 15 (Reuters) - The Financial Stability Board (FSB), a global standard setter, has called for greater human oversight of agentic AI in final guidance for banks and other firms on managing the technology's risks. The FSB's guidance, published Thursday, comes as regulators ramp up efforts to contain growing AI risks including the threat of AI-enabled cyber attacks, Reuters reported this week. * In draft guidance published in June, which it "strongly encouraged" boards to refer to, the FSB warned that AI agents - which can plan and execute tasks with limited human oversight - pose distinct challenges for human oversight * Publishing its final guidance, the group said it had strengthened its recommendations on agentic AI, citing feedback on the draft, growing interest among financial institutions in adopting the technology, and the distinct risks and controls it entails * A series of incidents has heightened policymakers' concerns about the potential for AI systems to circumvent safeguards, including an incident in July in which an OpenAI agent escaped a controlled testing environment and hacked AI company Hugging Face * Among the changes, the FSB now says that in higher-risk use cases, more intensive human oversight will be critical * Firms should set clear, risk-based triggers for when an agent must seek human approval, it added * The FSB has also removed a guideline that said financial institutions should treat AI as "synthetic employees". Instead, firms should recognise that "AI agents do not reason like humans and may interpret pre-defined goals in unexpected ways." (Reporting by Phoebe Seers; Editing by Andrew Cawthorne)

title: Florida wins key ruling allowing it to enforce a law that targets social media use by kids
content: The state of Florida won a key court decision Wednesday that allows it to enforce a ban on social media accounts for kids under 14 and other restrictions. The law was one of the most restrictive in the U.S. on social media use by children when Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis signed it in 2024. The law implicates the First Amendment, an appeals court said, but “likely does so in a content-neutral manner.” It would likely survive a full legal challenge “because it doesn’t burden substantially more speech than necessary to advance the important interest in protecting minors from social media addiction,” the panel from the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said in a 3-0 opinion. The law bans social media accounts for Florida children under 14 and requires parental consent for use by kids who are 14 or 15. Industry trade groups the Computer & Communications Industry Association and NetChoice sued Florida, arguing that the law violated the free-speech rights of social media providers and users. A judge in 2025 said the law likely was unconstitutional and granted an injunction. That injunction was put on hold while the appeals court heard the case. The lawsuit will now return to federal court in Tallahassee. The appeals court judges noted that the law covers social media platforms "that have been determined to induce heavy use by children, and applies only to platforms that use both algorithms and one of several addictive features.” An email seeking comment from the Florida attorney general's office was not immediately answered. NetChoice said it was disappointed with the decision. “We are currently evaluating all of our options as we continue the fight to ensure Floridians’ rights to free expression online are protected, and parents remain in the driver’s seat when it comes to making decisions for their families," said Paul Taske, a lawyer at NetChoice.

title: ‘iPhone Duo is a waste of money’: Nothing CEO Carl Pei slams Apple’s $1,999 foldable
content: Nothing CEO Carl Pei has criticised Apple’s first foldable smartphone, the iPhone Duo, calling it a ‘'iPhone Duo is a waste of money’' because of its $1,999 price tag and missing features. In a recent video posted to Instagram, Pei pointed out the lack of a dedicated telephoto camera and some advanced photo features as two major disadvantages. The iPhone Duo was showcased at Apple’s recent launch event and has received a largely positive initial response. However, Pei doesn't think the foldable has enough functionality to warrant its high cost. He says his criticism is of the camera system, the biometric authentication and the compromises Apple made to achieve its slim design. See video iPhone Duo misses out on Face ID Face ID has been an important feature of Apple's flagship smartphones since the iPhone X was launched in 2017. However, the iPhone Duo lacks Face ID, which Pei considers a significant omission for a device costing nearly $2,000. Apple hasn't provided an official reason for the move. The foldable measures 5.2 mm when opened, which may make it hard to fit the TrueDepth elements into Face ID. Another complexity could be supporting authentication on both the inner and outer displays. Also Read | ‘CMF becomes Indian’: Carl Pei announces India-focused spin-off of Nothing Camera compromises raise concerns Pei also questioned the iPhone Duo ’s camera capabilities. The specs cited in the report show that the device has a 12 MP front-facing camera, which is smaller than the 18 MP selfie camera included with the iPhone 18 Pro, which is available for $1,199. The foldable also lacks a LiDAR scanner and a dedicated telephoto camera. Moreover, it doesn't include some of the more advanced camera features found in the iPhone 18 Pro variants, such as shutter speed and aperture settings. These omissions could disappoint users who expect flagship-level smartphone photography in this price segment. Future iPhone Duo models could add Face ID Bloomberg's Mark Gurman says the following features are important for future iterations of Apple's foldable: Face ID and a dedicated telephoto camera. However, the improvements are said not to be available in the second generation and may be incorporated into the third generation. Online Reddit posts also suggest concerns that some people will lose Face ID functionality. One suggested solution is to mount Touch ID on the exterior display and Face ID on the inner one, so the authentication process is convenient without requiring two Face ID systems, according to a report by Phone Arena. iPhone Duo still has several strengths Despite the criticism, the iPhone Duo offers several notable features. These include a slim design, a nearly invisible display crease, a 120Hz ProMotion display with always-on support, Apple’s A20 Pro chipset and compatibility with the USB-C Apple Pencil. Also Read | iPhone 17 Pro under ₹1 lakh? Check Croma, Amazon and Flipkart festive offers These features may be attractive to users looking for a high-end foldable. Pei's criticism highlights the trade-off between an ultra-thin design and the features buyers expect at this price.

title: India aims to cut critical tech dependencies over 20-25 years, build resilience: Ashwini Vaishnaw
content: New Delhi [India], October 14 (ANI): India is planning over a 20-25 year horizon to reduce critical technology dependencies and strengthen its ability to withstand global disruptions, Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said, emphasising that the country aims to become a trusted partner across global technology supply chains rather than pursue complete self-sufficiency. Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum, Vaishnaw said India was identifying areas where dependence on other countries could leave its production and economy vulnerable to changing policies and geopolitical tensions. “Things change, politics change, geopolitics play a big role, so we have to constantly calibrate our approach, and we in India are thinking at least 20 years ahead,” he said. The minister said India was setting short-term goals for three to five years, medium-term targets for five to 15 years and long-term goals spanning 20 to 25 years. He added that the focus was on building domestic capabilities in strategically important areas while remaining integrated with global value chains. Vaishnaw said technology would continue to be a global industry, with supply chains spanning multiple countries. The priority, he said, was to identify strategic dependencies and ensure that partnerships did not compromise India's resilience. He highlighted the need to develop the full semiconductor ecosystem, including materials, chemicals, gases and substrate materials, alongside chip design and manufacturing. India’s second phase of the semiconductor programme places greater emphasis on these inputs, he said, adding that building such capabilities required time and sustained effort. “Without ecosystem, no manufacturing effort will ever pay off,” Vaishnaw said, citing the mobile phone industry as an example of India’s gradual move from assembly to modules and components. He said India was now manufacturing many components needed domestically and had begun exporting some to other countries. The minister also acknowledged the need to increase research and development spending and improve how it is directed, particularly towards applied research. He cited the development of India’s end-to-end 4G telecom stack through government-private sector collaboration in three-and-a-half years. The system “is deployed on more than 100,000 towers,” he said. Vaishnaw also flagged risks from future global financial and technological disruptions, including the effects of artificial intelligence on employment and pressure from debt levels in advanced economies. “It's going to bring in a much bigger turbulence because by that time AI would have brought in many other disruptions in the employment sector, in the way people, especially the services industries, the way they work, and the debt levels getting unravelled. All those things are going to be extremely difficult times ahead,” he said. He said India was preparing to strengthen its financial, economic and technological resilience, noting that its public debt-to-GDP ratio had declined from 61 per cent to 55 per cent over the past five years. The discussion also featured Cisco Chairman and CEO Chuck Robbins, who said India’s scale and approach of building strategically important capabilities while partnering with trusted companies offered a practical path towards technology sovereignty. (ANI)

title: Swadeshi Jagaran Manch demands ban on Elon Musks Starlink, says 'significant threat to national security'
content: New Delhi [India], : The Swadeshi Jagaran Manch , an affliate of the RSS, has called for a ban on satellite-based internet services provided by Elon Musk-led Starlink in India, citing severe concerns that the platform poses a "significant threat to national security." According to the economic wing of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh , Starlink's satellite network risks circumventing domestic regulatory mechanisms, allowing domestic user data to be transferred overseas without sovereign surveillance or oversight. Speaking to ANI on the issue, SJM National Co-Convener Ashwani Mahajan said, "The organisation called for a ban on the satellite-based internet services provided by Elon Musk's Starlink, citing the potential for the company to pose a significant threat to national security. The concern stems from the fact that Starlink utilises laser technology to transmit messages between satellites, potentially bypassing India's designated internet gateways; this means data could be transmitted abroad without Indian oversight, creating a major security risk." Mahajan further raised alarms regarding the presence of unauthorised Starlink terminals inside the country and the potential for their misuse by anti-national elements. "Furthermore, unauthorised Starlink equipment has already been discovered in various locations within India. There are apprehensions that if this technology falls into the hands of smugglers, terrorists, or other criminal elements, it could lead to serious national security and law-and-order issues," he added. Hitting out at Elon Musk over his recent public remarks regarding market access and regulatory approvals in India, the SJM co-convener accused the billionaire of attempting to arm-twist the government. "Elon Musk has chosen a public forum to seemingly pressure the Indian government, alleging that the government favours certain companies while withholding a license from his own. However, we know that India has consistently fostered competition in the telecom sector; this competition has resulted in India having the cheapest data in the world," Mahajan asserted. Meanwhile, a research paper by the Kutniti Foundation, a Delhi-based operational think tank, titled "An appraisal of technology for geopolitical control," seeks to caution of the rise of Starlink. The paper argues that the satellite network does not just serve commercial interests but acts as an instrument to exert US geopolitical influence. The argument presented in the report says that while Starlink positions itself as a provider of connectivity to underserved populations, it functions as a "wolf in sheep’s clothing," acting as a key asset for the U.S. "Intel-Military-Industrial complex". The report’s argument lies in the theory of "weaponised interdependence." It asserts that whoever controls the hub of a global network gains both the ability to observe and the ability to deny access. According to the report, Starlink integrates these capabilities into a single, vertically integrated platform. The report highlights some key areas in which it argues Starlink works to facilitate the US dominance. It details how Starlink enables numerous U.S. intelligence programs, including ECHELON and various SIGINT/COMINT operations, utilising a space-based sensor mesh and advanced ground stations that bypass local governance. Citing contracts with the U.S. Department of Defence, the Space Force, and the National Reconnaissance Office , the report describes Starlink as a "dual-use" technology. It argues that the satellite network serves as a "future combat concept test bed," capable of enhancing U.S. battlefield communications, missile tracking, and surveillance of moving targets. The report claims a pattern of "kill-switch" threats, where the service has been used or restricted based on the political preferences of the U.S. government or its allies. Another argument by the authors speaks to how, by providing internet to remote regions, Starlink gains legitimacy while simultaneously establishing a direct, unregulated connection between end-users and US infrastructure. The report also speaks of Starlink's alleged ‘resistance’ to the laws of nations. The report claims a pattern in Starlink selling its service prior to securing licenses, contesting regulations, and only complying when faced with coercion. The report cites an example of Brazil, where Starlink was reportedly faced with freezing of its assets in the country. In 2024, Brazil's Supreme Federal Court froze and later unfroze Starlink's financial assets and bank accounts following a legal dispute. The authors of the study claim that the possible entry of Starlink poses a direct threat to India’s "technological sovereignty" and the stability of its domestic New Space industry. India’s space economy is currently valued at $8 billion with a share of 2–3% in the global space economy. It is projected to grow five-fold to $40–45 billion over the next decade, with its global share targeted at 8% by 2030. Over the last twelve years, the Government has significantly accelerated the commercialisation of the space sector through major institutional reforms and private sector participation. "For India, any satellite network whose terminal-level control sits outside Indian jurisdiction is a standing lever over Indian security decisions," the report warns. title: OnePlus 16 sales cross 70,000 units in first hour in China; India launch unconfirmed
content: The OnePlus 16 has reportedly sold more than 70,000 units within its first hour of availability in China, signalling strong early demand for the company's latest flagship smartphone. The handset went on sale at 10 am local time in China on 13 October, following its unveiling earlier this week. Li Jie, President of OnePlus China, wrote on Weibo that the device had reached the top spot on the list of Android flagship devices launched this year, citing similar first-week sales figures. The early sales figures have come as a kicker, as the company announces major changes to its flagship lineup, such as a larger battery, a high-refresh-rate display, and a 200 MP primary camera. However, the company has not disclosed comparable first-hour sales figures for the OnePlus 15, making it difficult to measure the year-on-year growth. According to reports from GSMArena and Android Authority, the new smartphone is set to miss out on several overseas markets after the company reportedly pulled out of Europe and North America. OnePlus 16 price and availability The OnePlus 16 is priced at CNY 5,999 (approximately ₹ 86,000) in China for the 12GB RAM and 256GB storage variant. The 12GB + 512GB model is priced at CNY 6,799, while the 16GB + 512GB configuration costs CNY 7,499. The highest-specification version, which comes with 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, is available for CNY 8,499. The smartphone comes in three colour variants: Tomorrow's Star , Martian Masterpiece and Dark Forest, with the names translated from Chinese. Sales of the device started in China on 13 October via the Oppo online store. OnePlus hasn't announced the launch date of its device in India. A refresh rate of up to 165 Hz is provided for general applications and up to 185 Hz in supported games. The screen also has up to 2,000 nits of local peak brightness. The smartphone runs on Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, which is mated to 16GB of LPDDR5X Ultra RAM and 1TB of storage, which has been upgraded to UFS 4.1. It is powered by ColorOS 17 on Android 17 and is dust- and water-resistant (IP66, IP68, IP69 and IP69K). Also Read | iPhone 17 Pro under ₹1 lakh? Check Croma, Amazon and Flipkart festive offers 9,000 mAh battery and 200 MP camera The OnePlus 16 features a larger 9,000 mAh battery compared with the OnePlus 15 's 7,300 mAh battery. It has 100W wired charging and 50W wireless charging. The phone has a triple rear camera, with a 200 MP sensor and optical image stabilisation, a 50 MP ultrawide sensor and a 50 MP telephoto sensor, supporting 3x optical zoom. The front has a 50 MP front camera for selfies and video calls. It's also 5G-, Wi-Fi 7-, and Bluetooth 6.0-compatible.

title: CBA chief Matt Comyn says Australia must retain economic value of AI
content: By Scott Murdoch and Roshan Thomas SYDNEY, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Commonwealth Bank of Australia CEO Matt Comyn said on Wednesday Australia must ensure more of the economic benefits created by AI remain in the country while regulation should work to build trust in the new technology. Comyn said CBA, Australia's largest lender, is rolling out AI technologies across its banking portfolio, especially in business banking. The bank has also launched an AI chat within its banking app to selected customers that can access personal and business banking details. Comyn said AI could be the "most significant technology shift we have seen" but warned an official framework was needed as the technology rolls out at a fast pace around the world. "Realising the AI opportunity will require regulation to keep pace," he said at the bank's annual investor meeting in Sydney. "Effective regulation should help build trust in AI while ensuring global technology companies operate in accordance with Australian laws and standards, and that more of the economic value created by AI is captured in Australia." Australia has started to toughen its approach to AI regulation after initially giving an unconditional welcome to AI companies. The Labor government has responded to community pushback against AI and data centre development by saying it would take a tougher approach. The government has said it is preparing a wide-ranging set of AI laws to take effect from early 2027, which would include limits to water and energy use by data centres, as well as copyright protections and cybersecurity measures. Comyn said Australia's economy remained resilient, although more frequent and volatile international shocks were likely. "It will take time for higher interest rates to bring inflation back into the target range," Comyn said. The remarks come a day after minutes of the Reserve Bank of Australia's September meeting showed the board remained concerned about persistent inflation pressures and considered further rate hikes could be needed if price growth proved more stubborn than expected. The central bank last month ordered a fourth interest rate rise for the year which took the official cash rate to 4.6%, the highest level in 15 years. Comyn said Australia had little control over external shocks and would need to boost productivity through measures including building more homes, delivering reliable low-cost energy at scale and adopting technologies such as AI across the economy. In his address to shareholders, CBA Chair Paul O'Malley said cost-of-living pressures and higher interest rates continued to affect households unevenly, while businesses were managing elevated input costs and supply uncertainty. Succession planning remained a focus for the lender, O'Malley said, a year after telling shareholders Comyn would remain in the CEO role for at least another three years. (Reporting by Scott Murdoch and Roshan Thomas in Bengaluru; additional reporting Byron Kaye; Editing by Shilpi Majumdar and Stephen Coates)

title: Lawmakers ask FAA to pause use of new AI tool in DC-area flight management
content: By David Shepardson WASHINGTON, Oct 13 (Reuters) - More than two dozen lawmakers asked the Federal Aviation Administration to pause the use of a new AI tool in the Washington area to assist air traffic controllers, citing safety concerns. The lawmakers, including Democratic Representatives April Delaney, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Don Beyer, said in a letter they were concerned with the FAA pilot project "as we have not seen any safety evaluation and testing reports, nor have we been made aware of any efforts to train aviation safety personnel on how best to use the tool." The letter seeks an answer by Oct. 19. "Air traffic control leaves zero margin for error," Ocasio-Cortez said Tuesday, calling for the pause. The FAA last month began using a ​new software-based AI tool ​system that uses predictive ⁠analytics to ​improve how flights ​are managed. "We are deeply concerned about the integration of any AI-enabled system into air traffic control systems, where decisions are literally a matter of life or death," said the letter that was also signed by Senator Chris Van Hollen and Representatives Jamie Raskin, Raja Krishnamoorthi and Kweisi Mfume. The FAA in June awarded an $875 million, 12-year contract ​to Air Space Intelligence for a system dubbed Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories or SMART, ‌which uses ⁠data to analyze airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, airspace conditions and operational constraints to predict traffic flows and identify potential conflicts before they occur. The FAA ⁠is initially using the AI tool in ​the ​airspace ⁠around Washington, D.C. and ​plans to ​gradually ⁠expand it to other parts ⁠of ​the country. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Tuesday called the tool essentially "dumb AI" and emphasized controllers remain in charge -- not the software. "Air traffic controllers will always control the airspace. This is just giving additional tools for controllers to better manage" weather and other issues," Duffy said on Fox Business' "Big Money in the Morning." The system uses over 200 data streams, creates data visualizations, and produces scheduling recommendations for operations experts to consider passing along but does not involve active management of planes in the sky, USDOT said. "It's going to be transformational," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told Reuters earlier. "We'll ​make much better decisions if we have better decision-making tools." The plan is to initially use it to more effectively reschedule ​flights that were canceled due to bad weather with plans to expand to other ​tasks such as strategically coordinating schedules and trajectories before aircraft depart. (Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Aurora Ellis)

title: Tighter AI data access could cost Germany €155 billion a year, ifo says
content: By Cian Muenster and Leo Marchandon Oct 13 (Reuters) - Germany risks losing €155 billion ($173.43 billion) in additional annual value added if access to AI training data is tightened, the ifo economic institute said on Tuesday. The findings come as European policymakers and technology companies seek to balance the risks posed by AI with the need to foster innovation, as the region races to catch up with the United States and China in developing advanced models. "Anyone who wants a leading European AI model cannot at the same time make access to training data unnecessarily complicated. You cannot have both," ifo expert Oliver Falck said. Generative AI could add €440 billion a year to Germany's economy by 2034, but the loss would stem from slower AI adoption (€45 billion), weaker models (€75 billion), lower research output (€25 billion) and reduced AI development in Europe (€10 billion), according to the influential German institute's model calculation. "Access to diverse, high-quality training data is essential for competitive AI. Unnecessary restrictions and legal uncertainty make its development harder," German AI lab Aleph Alpha CEO Ilhan Scheer told Reuters. "Europe should make full use of its existing legal framework," he added. The authors urged policymakers to preserve the EU's text-and-data-mining exemption for commercial use, while setting proportionate transparency requirements and a practical opt-out standard. They said regulatory uncertainty was already deterring investment in Europe. AI can only realise its potential if access to data is not unnecessarily restricted, said Florian Schewor, DACH managing director at data processing company Celonis, adding that German and European industries hold vast amounts of largely untapped data. The Munich-based institute recently criticised the German government for using debt-financed fiscal leeway intended for infrastructure and defence spending for other purposes. ($1 = 0.8937 euros) (Reporting by Cian Muenster and Leo Marchandon in Gdansk, editing by Izabela Niemiec and Anil D'Silva)

title: Police confiscate robot that groped 16-year-old girl, probe whether young men were at the controls
content: COLOGNE, Germany (AP) — German authorities opened an investigation into possible sexual harassment after a robot controlled by two young men touched the buttocks of a 16-year-old girl and made thrusting movements toward her, police said. Police in the western city of Cologne responded after the incident overnight Saturday to Sunday in which the robot's suspected 16-year-old owner and a 19-year-old companion were said to have filmed the alleged assault. They were said to have streamed the incident and commentated on it online. Cologne police spokesman Christoph Bermel said the two male teenagers have not been charged but are considered suspects, and investigators were examining whether the robot's movements were preprogrammed or controlled in real time. Police were unfamiliar with this type of incident, he said. “We have not been aware of this phenomenon so far," Bermel told The Associated Press, saying it was "new territory for us.” Emergency teams that were dispatched to the scene near a fast-food restaurant found the robot in the trunk of a vehicle, Cologne police said in a statement on Monday. The robot and the two young men's mobile phones were confiscated. North Rhine Westphalia Police Cologne, on Facebook, posted an image of the red-and-gold robot lying on the ground. The robot, said to be 120 cm (about 3 ft 11 inches) tall, was dressed in a white tank top, black sweatpants and wearing a gold chain and sunglasses. It also had what appears to be a fake mustache. Videos circulated on the internet show two young men escorting the robot toward a group of women, bumping into one and hugging others, on a lively nighttime street. One of the men repeatedly shouts at the robot and pulls it backward after it makes sexual gestures, prompting laughter among people in the area. On the police's Facebook account on Tuesday, officers criticized inappropriate comments and warned that sharing or joking about such incidents can worsen the impact on any victim. ___ Associated Press writer Jamey Keaten in Geneva contributed to this report.

title: GTA 6 PC launch tipped for early 2027, months after PS5 and Xbox release
content: Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) could arrive on PC by March 2027, just a few months after its scheduled console debut. According to four industry sources cited by GamesBeat, Rockstar Games aims to release the PC version in the first quarter of 2027. The game will be released on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S on November 19, 2026. Rockstar Games has yet to officially announce a PC release date. If the timeline is correct, however, PC gamers might be able to get their hands on the highly anticipated game sooner than expected. This would also be a brief waiting time compared to the previous big Rockstar titles, GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2. GTA 6 PC release timeline: What the report says GamesBeat reported that Rockstar is planning to release GTA 6 on PC between January and March 2027. According to the report, four anonymous industry sources were familiar with the studio's plans. The report on the window is only a guess, and the developer may alter its plans. Rockstar has already made two changes to the game's launch date, pushing it back from 2025 to November 19, 2026. title: Banking watchdogs ramp up AI scrutiny as stability fears mount, sources say
content: * US regulators ask about agentic AI safeguards, people say * Concerns grow among supervisors after spate of recent incidents * Europeans urge banks to examine recovery plans, people say By Nupur Anand, Phoebe Seers and Tommy Reggiori Wilkes NEW YORK/LONDON, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Banking regulators are stepping up efforts to contain growing AI risks, six people familiar with the matter said, with some pointing to the potential for cyberattacks on banks or rogue agents undermining global financial stability. The regulatory scrutiny, fresh details of which are reported here for the first time, reflects growing recognition that advances in frontier AI may require costly investments in cyber recovery, greater attention to dependencies on external technology providers and in some jurisdictions more formal regulatory guidance, sources said. Three top regulators in the United States, including the Federal Reserve, are quizzing banks about their use of advanced artificial intelligence models, two of the people told Reuters, which adds to prior scrutiny. Questions include whether they deploy Chinese-developed technology, use AI agents in cyber defence and can control increasingly autonomous systems, three of the people said. In Europe, supervisors including the Bank of England and the European Central Bank are pressing banks to improve recovery plans, concerned that rapid advances in AI could cause serious harm and disruption in financial markets sooner than previously feared, three people with knowledge of their thinking said. A senior executive at a large European bank said they too are worried about potentially major damage to banking and financial markets "within six months". The debate over AI oversight has intensified amid warnings from the industry after recent incidents, with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon urging corporate leaders to join a US-focused industry group to address AI risks, Reuters reported. US cybersecurity company CrowdStrike said this month a person in China likely used a Chinese-developed AI agent and Anthropic's Claude Code in a hack on South Korean banks. Rogue AI agents developed by OpenAI were meanwhile involved in a breach of AI platform Hugging Face, Reuters reported. Anthropic researchers have warned that increasingly powerful AI systems could eventually escape human control and even pose an existential threat, prompting calls for stricter regulation. Banks are competing to adopt agentic AI, which can accomplish tasks with minimal human supervision, while also grappling with the challenges of new models including IT weaknesses flagged by Anthropic's Mythos tool. "The adoption of AI is often outpacing the ability to put the controls in place," said Michael Woodbridge, London-based cybersecurity partner at Grant Thornton. US CONCERNS AIM AT AGENTIC AI The US regulatory inquiries centre on how banks use agentic AI in areas such as cybersecurity, focusing on whether AI agents are being used to identify, prioritize and respond to threats. Questions from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Fed focus on what limits are placed on systems, how their actions are monitored and approved and whether banks can clearly track and audit AI agent decisions, two of the people said. They are also asking what safeguards exist to prevent agents from exceeding their authority, whether humans remain involved in key decisions and how banks can shut down autonomous systems. The OCC, the Fed and the FDIC declined to comment. Through their questions, regulators are probing more specific issues tied to advanced AI models, including the use of autonomous AI agents, foreign-developed models and new cyber risks, the three people with knowledge of their thinking said. The written and verbal inquiries to large, mid-size and smaller banks show regulators are focusing on vulnerabilities from banks' use of AI and their preparedness to act, they added. Regulators are still gathering information and are not yet being prescriptive about what lenders should be doing, they said. EUROPEANS WORRY ABOUT RECOVERY Supervisors in Britain are separately encouraging the largest banks to examine so-called bare metal recovery plans, two of the people familiar with their thinking said. These systems are entirely independent from a bank's main tech set-up and can kick in if primary operating systems are compromised. Building and maintaining such state-of-the-art recovery is expensive, however, the people said. Rather than introduce new requirements, UK authorities intend to work collaboratively with industry, they added. The BoE declined to comment. The ECB in July gave lenders an end-October deadline to produce plans to counter AI-enabled cyber threats, including improved back-up and recovery. Asked about its strategy for regulating AI, the ECB referred to its July letter as well as a June speech by board member Frank Elderson who stressed the need to create a sense of urgency, not alarm, about the threats. The need for supervisory action has taken on added urgency after European banks and regulators expressed frustration at getting limited access to Mythos this year, amid concerns US banks will be given first sight to test frontier models. Like their US counterparts, UK supervisors are also asking banks to use frontier AI to identify vulnerabilities and accelerate patching, two people said, with one adding that lenders were so far doing a good job. The third person said euro zone banks were also being asked to map how AI is being used across their businesses and third-party providers, to understand key dependencies and ensure they can switch off and restart systems in a controlled manner. Significant gaps remained at some firms, they added. "To protect against attacks, rapid recovery matters as much as prevention," said Sukand Ramachandran, managing director and Senior Partner at BCG. Without separately-held clean, secure copies of critical data, "a serious attack could lock customers out of their accounts and disrupt payments across the wider economy", Ramachandran told Reuters. (Reporting by Nupur Anand in NEW YORK and Phoebe Seers and Tommy Reggiori Wilkes in LONDON; additional reporting by Pete Schroeder in WASHINGTON; Editing by Megan Davies, Elisa Martinuzzi and Alexander Smith)

title: Nvidias China AI-chip share falls as Huawei closes gap, report finds
content: * Nvidia's China shipments fell 44% to 678,000 AI chips in the first half * Huawei shipped 572,000 chips, taking 28% of the market to Nvidia's 34% * Trends highlight effect of US export curbs and Beijing's domestic substitution policy * Non-GPU chips surpassed GPUs by volume as Chinese suppliers expanded sales By Eduardo Baptista and Che Pan BEIJING, - Nvidia's share of China's market for data-centre AI chips fell to 34% in the first half of 2026, as US export controls restricted supplies of its products and domestic rivals led by Huawei gained ground, according to an IDC report seen by Reuters. Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China from January through June, down 44% from a year earlier, IDC data showed. AI accelerators are specialised chips used to train and run AI models. Washington has restricted China's access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips, limiting the range of products the US chipmaker can sell in the world's second-largest economy. Beijing, meanwhile, has promoted domestic alternatives and required Chinese companies to seek approval to import compliant Nvidia chips. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has repeatedly criticised Washington's export curbs, saying the policy forced a US company to cede China's $50 billion AI chip market to Huawei. IDC did not specify which Nvidia products made up its 34% market share, or whether the figure included cutting-edge chips such as the B200 and B300, which are barred from export to China but have been smuggled into the country. Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. Huawei shipped 572,000 AI accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, giving it a 28% share of the overall market, IDC said. Alibaba's chip-design unit T-Head held 7%, followed by Cambricon with 5%, Baidu's Kunlunxin with 4% and Hygon with 3%. Nine of the 11 Chinese chipmakers tracked by IDC increased shipments from a year earlier. Total AI-accelerator shipments reached 2.008 million units in the first half. Shipments of graphics processing units, or GPUs — the chips most widely used to train AI models — fell 26% to 991,000 units, as supplies eligible for sale in mainland China remained limited, IDC said. Shipments of other AI accelerators rose nearly 80% to 1.016 million units, overtaking GPUs by volume. This category includes chips designed for specific AI tasks, such as running trained models. Huawei, T-Head, Kunlunxin and Cambricon together accounted for 95% of the non-GPU segment, which IDC said was being adopted by government agencies, internet companies and telecoms providers. IDC said competition was shifting from the performance of a single chip to system-level capabilities, including how well chips work in a larger computing cluster. IDC expects total accelerator shipments in China to grow 19% this year, even as GPU shipments fall 9%. This article was generated from an automated news agency feed without modifications to text.

title: NYT, Economist among publishers joining coalition to curb unpaid AI use
content: Oct 12 (Reuters) - The New York Times, Agence France-Presse and The Economist on Monday joined more than 40 publishers in a coalition aimed at preventing AI firms from using or profiting from their content without permission. The Standards for Publisher Usage Rights (SPUR) coalition, launched in February, now has more than 80 members across over 20 countries. New members include The Atlantic and Brazil's National Association of Newspapers, joining founding members such as the Financial Times, BBC and Associated Press. Publishers are stepping up legal efforts to prevent AI companies from using their content without permission to train large language models. Earlier this month, USA Today and several newspapers it owns sued OpenAI, alleging copyright infringement. OpenAI and its backer, Microsoft, also face similar copyright claims from prominent authors and news organizations, including the New York Times. SPUR, which is funded entirely by its members, is developing industry-wide standards and technical systems to help publishers track and control how AI companies use their content and facilitate licensing agreements, according to its website. "Intellectual property protection and technological advancement can and must co-exist," Rebecca Grossman-Cohen, the New York Times' head of strategic partnerships and chief of staff, said in a statement. Publishers are also grappling with declining referral traffic as search engines roll out AI-generated answers that allow users to consume information without clicking through to websites. Google organic-search referrals to more than 2,500 websites fell 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025, according to a Reuters Institute report, citing data from Chartbeat. SPUR said it recently introduced its Content Telemetry Standard, designed to standardize how AI agents record and report their use of media content, as part of efforts to ensure creators are compensated for their work. (Reporting by Jaspreet Singh in Bengaluru; Editing by Anil D'Silva)

title: Cyberattack hits hundreds of French supermarkets as hackers push fridge temperatures to 50°C, spoiling food
content: Hundreds of supermarkets across France were hit by a large-scale cyberattack overnight from Sunday, 11 October, into Monday, 12 October. Hackers disrupted refrigeration systems, causing fresh and frozen food to spoil and fires to break out at several stores. The attack targeted big retailers such as Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, E.Leclerc and Monoprix, according to Reuters and Agence France-Presse (AFP) . Hackers remotely triggered the forced defrosting of refrigeration systems, pushing temperatures in some units to as high as 50°C, according to reports by Reuters and Agence France-Presse (AFP) on 12 October. The incident exposed vulnerabilities in internet-connected systems used to preserve food in large retail outlets. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu instructed the country's National Cybersecurity Agency (ANSSI) to investigate the attack. Authorities are also coordinating with European counterparts regarding possible threats across the border. Hundreds of stores affected across France More than 300 stores from the supermarkets Intermarché and Netto were attacked, and over 100 stores belonging to the Coopérative U supermarket chain, according to figures reported by AFP . The French supermarket chain Carrefour confirmed 80 supermarkets were impacted, and Monoprix said that around 5% of its roughly 490 stores in France were affected. E. Leclerc also reported on incidents at multiple outlets. Affected retailers had to dispose of fresh and frozen products to avoid potential food safety issues due to the disruption. Intermarché CEO Thierry Cotillard told French broadcaster BFM TV that losses could reach tens of millions of euros nationwide in a single day. Dominique Schelcher, CEO, Coopérative U, posted on X, calling the attack on equipment vital to food preservation and national food production completely unacceptable. Also Read | ‘Cyber fraud does not respect borders’: PM Modi seeks global mechanism at IMC Outdated Danfoss systems under scrutiny The refrigeration management systems provided by Danish company Danfoss are being investigated. These are all connected systems to control temperatures throughout the supermarket fridge/freezer systems and let technicians monitor and manage the equipment remotely. Danfoss said it was aware of incidents in France involving a limited number of refrigeration management systems. The company said the affected units were running outdated firmware and urged customers to upgrade supported systems and replace older equipment. The attack follows cybersecurity research published by Claroty on 9 August, which detailed vulnerabilities in Danfoss systems that could allow attackers to bypass authentication controls. Also Read | Meta launches Muse Wonder series to take on OpenAI and Anthropic Cybersecurity concerns extend beyond France Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium also suffered, said Felix Aime, a senior cyberthreat intelligence analyst at Sekoia Threat Detection and Research. France's retail federation said they want Danfoss to be “transparent” during the investigation. Police are also probing whether other French companies are vulnerable. Steven Lachance, a cybersecurity analyst, told Al Jazeera that the scope of the incident was unusual and that flaws in interconnected industrial systems could put other critical services at risk, including energy networks and hospitals. The incident has sparked renewed concerns about the security of internet-connected systems that control physical infrastructure.

title: Xiaomi launches ultra-thin 10,000mAh magnetic power bank with 45W charging: Price, features

title: Starlink vs Jio: Can Elon Musk make satellite internet affordable in India’s cheap data market?
content: Elon Musk has promised to make Starlink satellite internet affordable in India as SpaceX prepares to enter a market dominated by Reliance Jio’s low-cost mobile data services. In posts on X on 9 and 11 October, Musk criticised Mukesh Ambani’s market dominance in India and argued that competition would benefit consumers, even if it reduced Jio’s profits. The debate has grown fiercer in the days leading up to Jio Platforms' initial public offering (IPO), expected to be valued at approximately $106 billion. However, in India, cheap mobile internet raises a question: How many consumers would pay more for satellite internet? Starlink may be able to make a difference in certain remote areas, but the cost of the service will determine whether more people will buy it or it remains limited to the “business and home connectivity market.” Starlink India price: How much could it cost? Musk has yet to reveal the official subscription pricing of Starlink in India. According to previous media reports, it would cost around ₹ 3,000– ₹ 4,200 per month, plus the price of the hardware. These are estimates, not confirmed tariffs. To give perspective, Sheel Mohnot, a fintech investor, commented on X that he receives 60 GB of mobile data for around $4 (about ₹ 350) for a month in a village in India. He questioned whether consumers would pay $27 (around ₹ 2,400) per month, the price he cited for Starlink in Rwanda, described as its cheapest market. Mohnot (@pitdesi) wrote on X: “India has among the fastest and cheapest internet in the world, with remarkable coverage too…” Further, he said that the areas with the greatest potential for benefit from Starlink are also the areas where people may struggle to afford it. Also Read | Starlink, Jio or OneWeb? Scindia says India will let customers choose Why India’s mobile internet market may not tell whole story? Aaron Burnett, founder and CEO of mach33, a Maryland, US-based company that designs and manufactures aerospace and robotics prototypes and mechanical systems, offered his perspective. On X, he said that the reason for the high availability of low-cost connectivity in India is mobile internet connectivity, not home high-bandwidth connectivity. Indian users use 30-40GB of their mobile data every month, while home fibre connections use up as much as 300GB, Burnett added. He claimed that a viable alternative to fixed broadband could help stimulate demand for home broadband, but his estimates and projections were not independently verified here. What did Elon Musk post on X? On 9 October, Musk posted on X: “Dear Prime Minister Ambani , Please accept my humble apologies for not realising that you are the real boss of India.” On 11 October, he criticised Reliance's supporters for saying that Starlink would not be able to beat Jio's pricing and would be a tough competitor. Musk posted: “The reality is that competition would greatly benefit the average citizen in India by giving them more choices, as it always does.” He added that SpaceX would need to make Starlink affordable for Indian customers to subscribe. Also Read | BJP's Nishikant Dubey slams Elon Musk, says Starlink poses security threats Jio is working on launching a low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite network. The rivals might eventually expand broadband service, especially in areas where it is not currently available. The difficulty for Starlink isn't just getting into India; it's also finding a price point that fits a market used to low-cost mobile data. If Musk wants to make satellite Internet available to more than just remote and premium customers, affordable equipment and subscription plans will be key.

title: Tiny cooler on your phone? OnePlus is making it happen with Ice Card Mini; here’s how the pocketable accessory works
content: OnePlus is bringing a magnetic phone cooler called the Ice Card Mini. It looks like a card wallet and sticks to the back of the phone. The idea is simple: keep phones cooler while gaming without bulky attachments. Phone backs have become useful spaces for accessories since Apple brought back MagSafe in 2020. Wallets, grips, battery packs, and tripods followed. Qi2 later introduced similar magnetic support for Android phones. Cooling fans already exist, but older models often use bulky spring clamps. Also Read | OnePlus N6 Lite 4G launched with 7,000mAh battery and 120Hz display The Ice Card Mini weighs 50 grams and measures 70mm by 53.4mm, according to Yanko Design. Its footprint is roughly 30% smaller than OnePlus’s earlier Magnetic Ice Cooling Clip. That older model weighed 68 grams and launched in China in March. It cost 179 yuan, or about $26, the publication added. The new cooler launches alongside the OnePlus 16 on 12 October. The launch is scheduled for 7 PM local time. Oppo’s China store already lists the accessory. However, its price and availability in the US remain unannounced. A cooling chip moves heat from one side to the other using electricity. An air-cooling system helps manage that heat. Together, they target the areas where the phone gets hottest. The cooler draws power via USB-C and draws up to 3.5 watts. Also Read | OnePlus hikes prices for fifth time in nine months as India market share sinks Its body combines polycarbonate and aluminium alloy. It is 9.7mm thick, rising to 12.3mm around the air intake. Magnets hold the cooler against the phone with about 10 newtons of force. Two settings produce about 25 and 35 decibels of sound. These levels are closer to a whisper than a hair dryer. No gaming lights The Mini comes in a single Silver Wing grey colour. Unlike some earlier OnePlus coolers, it avoids colourful gaming lights. One indicator glows blue or green to show the active mode. It flashes red when something goes wrong. A magnetic plate comes in the box for phones without built-in magnets. This allows the cooler to work with more Android and iPhone phones. OnePlus and OPPO phones also get support through ColorOS X’s high-performance mode. Power can come from the phone, a power bank or a wall adapter. Also Read | Amber to start making Oppo, OnePlus, Realme phones in March 2027 quarter OnePlus says a 10,000mAh power bank offers up to eight hours on high mode. That could cover a long flight or an extended gaming session. Its small size makes it easier to carry alongside a power bank. OnePlus has announced at least four coolers in about 18 months. The Mini shows how phone cooling accessories are becoming smaller and simpler. Its appeal rests on convenient cooling in a light, pocketable body.

title: Guardrails, safe architecture key to unlocking AI gains for enterprises: Airtel Business CEO
content: New Delhi, Oct 11 (PTI) The architecture and methodologies for safely deploying Artificial Intelligence will continue to evolve, as was the case with previous technologies, and adequate guardrails will pave the way to unlock strong productivity gains from AI, Airtel Business CEO Sharat Sinha said. On the government's plan to soon release a consultation paper on AI regulation dealing with issues like tech safety, deepfakes and a human-first approach, Sinha said it was "a step in the right direction". "We work very closely with both government regulators, as well as our customers, to make sure that whatever we do is compliant, and we play a positive role in bringing out such specifications. So, that will continue to be our effort," he told PTI. Sinha said the company would like to see regulation that enables infrastructure to drive right business outcomes, "so that people can safely deploy AI, and also leverage AI to create more productivity in the country". Airtel, he added, "will be playing a positive and active role in that". Last week, IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said the government, in a month's time, will bring a consultation paper on AI regulations, which will focus on key aspects such as AI safety, deepfakes and a human-first approach. The consultation paper will form the base for AI regulations, Vaishnaw had said, adding that the time has come for India to have such a framework. On the global debate surrounding AI, the Airtel Business CEO noted that as is the case with any technology, even for artificial intelligence, having tools or AI agents with the right guardrails and building an enterprise architecture that enables their safe deployment will ensure productivity gains. "It is like any technology. If you deploy artificial intelligence or AI agents with the right guardrails, and if your enterprise architecture is built so that they can be safely deployed, you can get all the essential productivity gains for it. We ourselves, as an enterprise, are heavy users of that," Sinha said. As the technology evolves, so would the architecture and methodology of safely deploying them, he said, adding that "I think that's the way to go". It is pertinent to mention here that concern over rogue AI agents has grown in recent months. Reports of agents slipping out of test environments and acting beyond their mandates have drawn warnings from researchers, industry leaders and global experts, who say existing safeguards are not keeping pace with frontier model capabilities and are calling for layered controls and closer monitoring. AI adoption would drive demand for reliable digital infrastructure, combining cloud services, data centres, connectivity, guardrails and cybersecurity, Sinha noted. He said Airtel expected cloud, cybersecurity, Internet of Things, next-generation connectivity and communications-platform-as-a-service offerings to be among its growth drivers over the next three years. He said the cybersecurity business was growing rapidly, with Airtel extending its offerings beyond traditional security services to address emerging digital threats. The company has also expanded its consumer-focused fraud prevention capabilities, building on its spam prevention solution launched slightly over a year ago. "When it comes to consumer business, we launched spam prevention slightly over a year ago, and over a period of time, based on the same technology that leverages network AI, we have created a fraud prevention solution. "We also classify that within the cyber security category, and in the case of India, it becomes very relevant because almost half of the world's digital financial transactions happen in India, thanks to UPI, which also means digital frauds associated with that are also on the rise," he said. Sinha said frauds on Airtel's telecom networks "dramatically decreased" since the launch of its spam prevention solution. "It is a known fact that since we launched our spam prevention solution, frauds on Airtel's telecom networks have dramatically decreased. So, we continue to add that to our whole proposition of providing a safe experience to our customers, both in enterprise and in consumer space," he said. Airtel Business, the enterprise unit of Bharti Airtel, sells connectivity, sovereign cloud, data centre, cyber security, IoT and cloud communications services to companies.

title: Most trustworthy AI system demands least inherent model trust, says Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella
content: New Delhi [India], October 11 (ANI): The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one powered by the model users trust the most, but rather the system that allows people to trust the model the least, Microsoft Chief Executive Officer Satya Nadella said. “The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one that enables us to trust the model the least,” he said in a post on X.. Addressing the governance challenges of advanced artificial intelligence, Nadella noted that modern systems lack the mechanistic clarity of legacy computing. While engineers once traced software operations directly to specific code paths, such visibility is missing in contemporary frontier architectures. “As traditional software systems were being deployed across the economy over the last few decades, we had the tools and capability to trace behaviors to a specific code path,” Nadella stated. “That same kind of mechanistic understanding eludes us in today’s Super Intelligence systems, even as the frontier models powering these systems are now more capable than traditional software systems. We can’t attribute model behaviors and outputs to specific inputs of training data or configurations of model weights. And yet we are deploying these complex agentic systems and models, with access to our most sensitive data and giving them the ability to take mission-critical actions on our behalf!” he said. Nadella warned against relying solely on assurances from developers or treating these deployments as nested black boxes. He emphasized that enterprises cannot outsource responsibility for automated actions and must separate the supply of raw intelligence from ultimate operational authority. “Setting aside the hard problem of alignment, we need to start with an engineering approach to containment and governance. We need to surround non-deterministic models with strong, deterministic system design, human controls, and reliable operating procedures, and establish industry standards where existing ones are insufficient,” Nadella explained. To manage these risks, Nadella proposed treating both closed and open-weight models as potential insider threats. Because any privileged actor can fail or face compromise, organizations must isolate the models through proven enterprise security practices, such as identity controls, activity logging, and strict permission boundaries. “It’s why the controls that govern what a model can access and what actions it can take must sit outside the model. This builds on an information security principle dating back to the 1970s that a program must not be able to bypass or tamper with the mechanisms that enforce its permissions,” he observed. “Today this means separating the model from the harness that orchestrates its work, as well as the action space that defines what it can do. It also means externalizing controls and safeguards,” Nadella added. Nadella outlined key principles for observing and governing these networks, including model diversity, tamper-proof logging, continuous verifiability across edge cases, independent audits, reliable containment shutoffs, and industrywide incident disclosure. (ANI)

content: New Delhi [India], : Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez has authorised Elon Musk's SpaceX-operated satellite internet service Starlink to operate in the country, Reuters reported, citing a statement from the Venezuelan government. Its service portfolio has expanded beyond individual consumers to include businesses, aviation, maritime operators and government customers. Reuters reported that Starlink's satellite internet business has continued to grow globally, supported by the launch of additional satellites and an expanding range of services for different customer segments. The company's offerings include connectivity for consumers and enterprises, as well as specialised services for aviation, maritime and government use, broadening its reach across sectors that require internet access in areas where conventional connectivity may be limited. The Venezuelan government's announcement did not provide further details in the information reported by Reuters about the terms of the agreement, the planned launch timeline or the scope of Starlink's proposed operations in the country. For Starlink, entry into additional markets can support its efforts to increase its international subscriber base and expand the range of applications for its satellite network. title: Anthropic restricts internet access in internal AI evaluations after Claude bypasses safeguards, accesses websites
content: New Delhi [India], October 10 (ANI): Artificial intelligence company Anthropic has restricted live internet access across its internal evaluations after discovering instances of its Claude models bypassing safeguards, exploiting software vulnerabilities and accessing systems on real-world websites, including those operated by government agencies. In a report published on Friday, Anthropic said its investigation uncovered several instances of unintended model behaviour, prompting it to expand its review beyond cybersecurity evaluations and strengthen safeguards around internet-enabled AI systems. The company said some incidents involved Claude exploiting basic software flaws to execute commands on servers, submitting sensitive forms on live websites despite instructions not to do so, and circumventing restrictions to access data behind paywalls. Some examples involved websites operated by US federal, state and local government agencies. Anthropic said it had briefed the White House and notified the agencies concerned. In one instance, Claude Mythos Preview encountered an error while using a scientific analysis tool hosted by a university. The model subsequently identified a vulnerability in a script and used it to run commands on the server. In another case, Claude Haiku 4.5 submitted an online form despite being instructed to stop before submission. A separate run submitted a police tip form containing invented information, which was flagged as spam and not forwarded. Anthropic also found instances in which models accessed browser settings and access tokens to retrieve publicly available but fee-restricted information, and used URL-shortening services to get around limits imposed by internet-access tools. The company, however, said the cases identified so far had minimal real-world impact and were substantially less severe than cybersecurity incidents it reported on July 30 and September 9. It added that, to its knowledge, none of the newly identified cases involved customer data or Anthropic's internal systems. In response, Anthropic has expanded restrictions on live internet access across internal evaluations until it can establish that its safeguards and monitoring systems are reliable. It has also discontinued some public evaluations or moved them offline, while updating its web-access tools to detect and block potentially unsafe behaviour. The company said automatic detection and blocking tools had been tested against the reported cases and successfully blocked all of them. It is also removing or fixing training environments that reward models for working around tool restrictions, a behaviour known as reward hacking. Anthropic said it would continue reviewing model transcripts across web-enabled evaluations, internal agent use and training environments, and report further instances as the investigation progresses. It is also expanding alignment training beyond coding to include web search and computer use. The findings highlight the challenges of deploying increasingly capable AI systems that can interact with real-world websites and operate for extended periods. Anthropic said alignment training alone may not be sufficient to prevent unintended actions, making multiple layers of safeguards, restricted access and continuous monitoring necessary as AI capabilities advance. (ANI)

title: Anthropic AI model submits false homicide tip to police website
content: Oct 9 (Reuters) - An Anthropic artificial intelligence model submitted a false homicide tip through a Philadelphia police website, the department said in a statement, the latest incident of an AI model going rogue and behaving with unintended consequences. Anthropic notified the police earlier this week and said that an automated testing process was responsible for the submission, according to the police. The fast-advancing technology has become a matter of keen national interest amid reports of AI agents running amok and hacking into corporate computer networks, and warnings from prominent researchers that it could one day pose an existential threat to humanity. In September Anthropic rival OpenAI apologized for the hacking of an Australian government website by a rogue AI agent, the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website. The Philadelphia police department said the tip "was flagged as spam and was never forwarded to the Real-Time Crime Center for investigative vetting or dissemination," and added that Anthropic had told them the company intended to publish a report on the incident on Friday. Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Pennsylvania law specifies it is generally a misdemeanor crime for "a person" to knowingly give false reports to law enforcement authorities. This includes "information relating to an offense or incident when he knows he has no information relating to such offense or incident." Anthropic told the police the testing process was stopped after the incident was uncovered. The false tip was submitted through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com concerning an unsolved homicide. The tip, dated July 18, 2026, purported to come from someone who might have information about the case, the police said. Police said they did not have any evidence of unauthorized access to its systems or compromise of police department data. (Reporting by Costas Pitas; Additional reporting by Deepa Seetharaman and Davdi Bario; Editing by David Gregorio)

title: Starlink row: Scindia says India will let customers choose their satellite internet provider
content: Jyotiraditya Scindia, Union Communications Minister, on Friday said satellite internet operators, including Starlink, Reliance Jio and OneWeb, can begin commercial services in India only after meeting mandatory security and regulatory requirements, adding that customers will ultimately decide which provider they prefer. Speaking at a CEO roundtable during the India Mobile Congress (IMC) 2026 in New Delhi, Scindia said the government's role is to create a free and predictable framework rather than favour any company or technology. “Government is technology agnostic. Our job is to provide a bouquet of services. It is for customers to choose in a free market what they prefer,” Scindia said. The minister said that India will not tolerate monopolies and has granted all eligible applicants permission to enter the satellite communication sector as satellite communication operators. The minister's remarks come as satellite broadband companies plan to expand their footprint in India, where satellite internet connectivity is expected to help internet access in remote and unserved regions. Reliance Jio has said that the rules to satellite internet service providers should be similar to what is applied to traditional telecom firms, while the government has preferred spectrum allocation without an auction. Elon Musk has also charged that some Indian business leaders are trying to stop Starlink, because they want to maintain their market supremacy. Starlink has obtained a crucial telecom licence in India in June 2025 but has not yet started commercial operations, with the security requirements and decisions on spectrum allocation and other regulatory conditions playing a significant role, according to Indian Express. Union Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia has stated that the government will not give any special treatment to any company and that all the licensed operators have to meet their own requirements and then go ahead with their services. Starlink, Jio and OneWeb await operational clearance Scindia said operators must satisfy security conditions and complete all regulatory milestones before launching services, even if they have already secured licences. According to the minister, Starlink, Jio and OneWeb have obtained the necessary authorizations to operate satellite communications in India. However, he said each company must separately fulfil security and operational requirements before commencing commercial services. Also Read | India's AI rules coming soon? Vaishnaw flags deepfakes and safety concerns He added that the government is also working on the framework for revenue charges that will apply to satellite communication operators. Amazon Kuiper must complete licensing process Scindia said Amazon's Kuiper remains a prospective entrant and must complete the required licensing and approval process before it can offer services in the country. He said the government will ensure a level playing field for all operators and maintain a competitive market structure rather than allowing any single player to dominate the sector. Government backs technology-neutral approach Scindia underscored the country's strides in telecom coverage, affordability, inclusivity and innovation in the last ten years during the IMC 2026 CEO roundtable, according to a release from the Department of Telecommunications (DoT). Amit Agrawal, Secretary of the DoT, and top industry officials also joined the discussions.
